extracted.intended_audience: early-career researchers and grant applicants (PhD candidates, postdocs, junior PIs)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for researchers on understanding grant rejections and improving/resubmitting funding applications; focuses on diagnosing non-scientific causes of failure and practical steps to increase success in future rounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit to funding call / scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure your application fits the funding agency's requirements and the specific call; avoid submitting to calls where the scope only very loosely fits the project.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author warns that people sometimes apply to loosely related calls in hopes of a 'stroke of luck' and that rejection from a low-expectation application can be blamed on the funder's strict boundaries. Example given: 'cancer therapeutics' can be a very broad and misleading definition. Aligning scope to the call reduces easy grounds for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and conciseness of writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing should be clear and concise so reviewers can readily understand the project and its importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post assumes clear, concise writing is a baseline; even when the science is strong, poor communication can harm ranking. Workshops and seminars emphasize communication style as integral to grant success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific quality and novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying science must be solid and, where possible, ground‑breaking or of high merit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author notes that in higher tiers of rankings scientific quality is often comparable across applications, so merit is necessary but not always sufficient—other factors (presentation, fit) then determine which proposals are funded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research the audience / funder priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: Thoroughly research the audience (funding agency officers and reviewers), including previously funded projects and areas of expertise, to align your application to their interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowing what the funder has supported previously and the reviewers' backgrounds helps tailor the proposal. The post recommends using this research to align emphasis and possibly adapt the project framing to fit funder priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sell your project (marketing and persuasion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the grant application as a marketing effort: persuade reviewers that your project is the best investment by tailoring message and communication style to the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that funded PIs are often those who are better at presenting and selling their projects. Communication style and the ability to project a 'bright scenario' influence funding decisions as much as the science itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match between project and environment / lab fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasize the fit between the project and the host lab/institution, showing the environment is ideal for delivering the proposed research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding agencies choose applications that portray a great project being undertaken in the ideal environment. Demonstrating that the lab has the necessary expertise, resources, and track record strengthens the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set ambitious but feasible goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Propose goals that are both ambitious and realistic — ambitious enough to be exciting, but feasible enough to be believable and achievable within the project's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post cautions against making claims that cannot possibly be fulfilled. Agencies prefer ambitious yet credible aims rather than overreaching promises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Articulate plausible impact and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: Describe the expected results and their implications clearly, aiming for impact across a reasonable number of conditions without claiming far‑fetched broad applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests framing results as having implications for 'a number (but not a far-fetched collection) of conditions' to avoid implausible breadth while still demonstrating significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to misunderstandings (clarifications or rebuttals)
rubrics_metrics.description: When appropriate, request clarification from the agency or submit a rebuttal/explanation to address misunderstandings in review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A request for clarification or a rebuttal letter can be constructive and may result in additional input. Use this mechanism to correct factual misunderstandings rather than as an emotional reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterate and tailor for resubmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Learn from rejection feedback and tailor the application for the next round rather than simply resubmitting the same proposal unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grant calls recur and many encourage re‑submission. The author advises analysing what made winning applications successful and improving your own application accordingly instead of blindly repackaging it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish collaborations to improve fit
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider creating new collaborations or partnerships that make your proposal a better fit for a particular funding agency or call.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If researching the funder reveals gaps in expertise or priorities, forming collaborations can help align your project with reviewer expectations and funder missions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain professionalism; avoid public ranting/blame
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep reactions to rejection professional; venting/blaming (e.g., 'reviewer #3') should be limited to early private stages and not interfere with constructive next steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author acknowledges that ranting can be liberating initially but recommends moving past it to focus on productive responses—complaining publicly or fixating on perceived unfairness is counterproductive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of the funding climate and manage expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand acceptance rates and broader funding trends to set realistic expectations about chances of success and to inform strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece uses acceptance‑rate anecdotes (e.g., Switzerland) and notes the impact of funding crises on allocation. Awareness of funding scarcity helps contextualize rejections and shape pragmatic approaches (timing, target agencies).
